build time. No runtime fetch, no analytics — the source's beacon plumbing is left behind. The
loop is commit-before-peek: the reader guesses, THEN the world answers, and the gap is the

personas.label: For people who build things
personas.invite: You already run a loop when you build: sketch a guess, run the thing, read what it actually did. Five short passes, one guess each. No pitch until the end.

cards.question: You are about to open a page you have never seen. Commit to what you think it is before it shows you anything. Which one do you expect?

choices.label: A pitch dressed up as a demo
choices.peek: There is no pitch on this screen. It is a small working thing that only moves when you commit to a guess first. You just committed, which is the whole point: you never arrive at anything blank, you arrive already leaning.
choices.found: that you never arrive blank, you arrive already leaning

choices.label: A tool I can actually run and read
choices.peek: Close. It is a small working thing that only moves once you commit to a guess. Notice what you just did: you wrote a spec for this page before a single line of it loaded, because you always hold a model before the evidence shows up.
choices.found: that you held a model before the evidence showed up

choices.label: I genuinely have no idea
choices.peek: Even that is a guess: you predicted your own uncertainty. When you spin up something unfamiliar you are never truly blank, you carry a rough model in, then let the run correct it. That rough model is what everything here builds on.
choices.found: that even no idea was a model you carried in

cards.question: You wrote the spec in your head. Before you read the actual output, commit again: when you peek at what this page really did, will it match the version you pictured?

choices.label: Close enough, roughly what I pictured
choices.peek: Peeking is the check. The version in your head was a model; the thing on the screen is the run. Reading the run is not a formality, it is the only way to find where your model and reality stopped agreeing.
choices.found: that reading the run is the only way to find where the model and reality parted

choices.label: Probably off in some way I cannot name yet
choices.peek: That instinct is worth trusting. You cannot know how your model is wrong until you look at the actual behavior, not the behavior you assumed. The peek is you opening the log instead of trusting the plan.
choices.found: that you opened the log instead of trusting the plan

cards.question: Something you just read landed a little off from your spec. Commit before you look closer: is that gap a bug in your build, or is it the most useful thing on the screen?

choices.label: A gap means I got it wrong
choices.peek: Flip it. A gap between expected and actual is not a verdict on you, it is a reading that points exactly at the part of your model that needs work. The bigger the surprise, the more it just told you.
choices.found: that the bigger the surprise, the more it just told you

choices.label: The gap is the useful part
choices.peek: Right. The diff between what you expected and what actually ran is pure signal. A run that matches your model perfectly teaches you nothing new; the mismatch is where all the information lives.
choices.found: that the mismatch is where all the information lives

choices.label: Depends how big the gap is
choices.peek: Good calibration. The size of the gap is the size of the message: a small surprise is a small correction, a large one says your model was aimed wrong. Either way it is data pointing somewhere, never a failing grade.
choices.found: that the size of the gap is the size of the message

cards.question: You have a real gap in hand and it is pointing somewhere. Commit before you decide: what is the smartest move with a gap this size?

choices.label: Rewrite the whole thing to be safe
choices.peek: Rarely worth it. The gap already told you which part of your model was off, so you patch that part and rerun, not the rest. Learning here is just closing the gap, made small and cheap so you can do it again in a minute.
choices.found: that learning is just closing the gap, small and cheap

choices.label: Adjust the one thing the gap pointed at, then rerun
choices.peek: That is the move. You change the piece the surprise implicated, run it again, and read the new gap. Do it in tight cheap passes and your model tracks reality closely, because you never let the gap grow stale.
choices.found: that tight cheap passes keep your model tracking reality

cards.question: You ran the same short circuit four times: guess, read the run, size the gap, adjust. Before the last reveal, commit: is that circuit a beginner habit you outgrow, or is it what good building actually is?

choices.label: A habit for when I am learning something new
choices.peek: It never stops being the work. Predict, check, adjust is not scaffolding you throw away once you are good; it is the shape of every skilled build, run tighter and faster as your models sharpen. We work the exact same loop, out in the open, on the hard problems people bring us.
choices.found: that predict, check, adjust is the shape of every skilled build

choices.label: It is just what good building is
choices.peek: That is it. Predict, check, adjust, cheaply and often, is what competent building has always been under the names. We run this same loop in the open on the hardest thing you can hand us, and we show our gaps instead of hiding them.
choices.found: that we run this same loop in the open and show our gaps

personas.label: For beginners
personas.invite: You do not need any background to be here. This page is a small quiet thing that only asks you to guess before you look. If a short story helps a lesson stick, you already know how to use this.

cards.question: A ferryman crosses a wide river every morning with a rope tied between two trees on either bank. Before you hear what the rope is for, commit to a guess: why do you think he keeps it?

choices.label: So the boat cannot drift away in the current
choices.peek: That is part of it, but not the whole thing. The rope is also how he knows, mid crossing, whether the river is pulling harder than yesterday. He feels the tug through his hands before his eyes ever tell him.
choices.found: that his hands felt the river before his eyes saw it

choices.label: So passengers have something to hold
choices.peek: Warm answer, but not quite. The rope is his early warning. When it pulls harder than usual against his grip, he already knows the current shifted, and he leans into the oar before the boat starts sliding.
choices.found: that a small pull in his hands warned him early

choices.label: I honestly do not know yet
choices.peek: That is a fine place to start. The rope is his early warning. He feels the river through it and knows, before he can see it, whether today is a normal day or a harder one. You just did the same thing: you guessed before you knew, and that is the whole lesson.
choices.found: that guessing before you knew was already the lesson

cards.question: A baker tastes her dough once before it rises and once after. Before we say why, commit to a guess: what is the first taste actually for?

choices.label: To check that she used the right ingredients
choices.peek: Closer than it looks. The first taste is her guess of what the finished bread will be. The second taste is the one that tells her. If the two tastes disagree, she learned something about her flour, or her yeast, or her hands that day.
choices.found: that her first taste was already a quiet guess about the second

choices.label: So she can tell later if something changed
choices.peek: Right on. The first taste is a note to her future self. Without it, the second taste has nothing to compare to. With it, she can feel exactly where the dough went somewhere she did not expect.
choices.found: that a note to her future self let her feel the difference

choices.label: Just habit, I would guess
choices.peek: Sometimes habits carry a hidden lesson. Her first taste is a quiet guess; the second is the taste that tells her. She never has to say those words to be doing exactly that, and neither do you.
choices.found: that a quiet habit was doing the work of a guess

cards.question: A mapmaker draws a river from a hilltop, then walks down and follows it. Before we finish the story, commit: what is the walk for, if he has already drawn the map?

choices.label: To make the map prettier with more detail
choices.peek: Not the main reason. The walk is how he finds where the drawing was wrong. Every bend that surprises him is a small correction he can pencil in. Without the walk, the map is only his hope of the river.
choices.found: that every surprising bend was a correction the walk gave him

choices.label: To find where his drawing does not match
choices.peek: Just so. On the walk he finds where the drawing was off. He drew what he thought the river was, then let the river tell him where he was wrong. That gap between drawing and river is not a failure of his map; it is the map getting better.
choices.found: that the gap between drawing and river was the map getting better

choices.label: Because sometimes you just need to walk
choices.peek: Gentle, and also true. On the walk he notices where the river disagrees with his drawing, and he lets those small disagreements teach him. That is the whole practice, no bigger words needed.
choices.found: that letting small disagreements teach you is the whole practice

cards.question: Look at the room you are in. Before you look again more carefully, commit to a guess: how many things in your line of sight are colored blue?

choices.label: Fewer than I will actually count
choices.peek: Very likely. Now that you guessed low, your eye will find one or two more than you expected. That small surprise is the whole thing you came here to feel: your guess and the room disagreed a little, and the disagreement taught you something.
choices.found: that the small disagreement between guess and room taught you

choices.label: About the same, roughly
choices.peek: That is a confident guess about your own room. If you look and it matches, you already knew your room well. If it is a little off, that small gap is the only place learning happens, and you just made room for it.
choices.found: that a small gap is the only place learning actually happens

choices.label: More than I will actually count
choices.peek: Interesting bet. Now the second look has weight. Whether your count comes in under, over, or right on, you guessed first so the room could answer you back. That is all this practice is: guess, then look.
choices.found: that guessing first let the room answer you back

cards.question: You just did the same small thing four times: with the ferryman, the baker, the mapmaker, and your own room. Before we say it back to you, commit to a guess: what do you think you were quietly practicing the whole time?

choices.label: Guessing first, then looking
choices.peek: Yes. That is the whole thing. You guessed before you knew, then you let what was really there answer you back. When your guess and the world agree, the day is calm. When they disagree a little, that small gap is where you learned something. You do not need any bigger word for it than that.
choices.found: that guessing first, then looking, was the whole practice

choices.label: Paying closer attention than usual
choices.peek: Warm and close. The attention was there, but the trick was the order. You guessed first, and only then looked. The guess is what made the look able to teach you anything. Without the guess, the look is just seeing; with it, the look becomes learning.
choices.found: that the guess is what let the look teach you

choices.label: Letting small surprises teach me
choices.peek: Just so. Every one of the four little stories had the same shape: someone guessed, then something answered back, and the small surprise in between was where the learning lived. You do not have to hunt for big surprises. The small ones, if you meet them on purpose, are enough.
choices.found: that small surprises, met on purpose, are enough to learn from

personas.label: For students
personas.invite: If you have taken a lab class, a stats unit, or a psych chapter, you already have the reflex this page rewards. It is a study aid more than a course. Every step is opt in, and the math at the end is a reward for curiosity, not a gate to pass.

cards.question: You are about to run a small titration in AP Chemistry. Before your teacher tells you what the endpoint should look like, commit to a guess: how many drops of base do you think it will take to turn the flask pink?

choices.label: About what the textbook example showed
choices.peek: Fair anchor. The textbook example is your first guess at the answer. When your actual drop count comes in high or low, the difference tells you something specific about your acid, your base, or your reading of the color change, not that you got it wrong.
choices.found: that the difference between textbook and flask tells you something specific

choices.label: A little more than the textbook example
choices.peek: A calibrated guess. You just did the thing a good lab notebook records at the top: your expected result. If the flask surprises you, the surprise is where the actual lesson of the day is going to live.
choices.found: that your expected result is where the lesson gets to land

choices.label: I want to run it and see
choices.peek: That instinct is right for a lot of labs, but write the number down first anyway. Without a guess on paper, the run cannot surprise you, and a lab without surprise is just a recipe. Even a rough guess earns you the surprise.
choices.found: that a rough guess on paper earns you the surprise later

cards.question: In AP Statistics you plot heights of 30 classmates. Before you look at the histogram, commit: what shape do you think it will roughly have?

choices.label: A clean bell curve
choices.peek: A reasonable first bet. With only 30 people it will be lumpier than a textbook bell, and that lumpiness is not noise you should dismiss. The gap between the clean shape you predicted and the actual shape is exactly what small samples teach you.
choices.found: that the lumpiness of a small sample was the lesson itself

choices.label: Two bumps, since teenagers vary a lot
choices.peek: Interesting guess. If the histogram comes back with one bump instead, your expectation about how much teenagers vary just got corrected by 30 measurements. That is what a sample is for: it corrects the guess you brought in.
choices.found: that the sample corrected the guess you brought in

choices.label: I have no strong shape in mind
choices.peek: Then write down the vaguest version of your guess anyway: about symmetric, one bump, medium spread. Even a soft prediction gives the run something to disagree with. Otherwise the histogram is just a picture, not a lesson.
choices.found: that even a soft prediction gave the picture something to teach you

cards.question: In AP Biology you predict a cell will double in about 24 hours. It doubles in 30. Before you look up why, commit: what does that 6 hour gap actually mean?

choices.label: My prediction was wrong and I should discard it
choices.peek: Do not discard it, learn from it. A 6 hour gap is a felt signal that points at exactly which part of your guess to look at first: nutrient supply, temperature, the cell type. The gap is the pointer, not the failing grade.
choices.found: that the gap was a pointer, not a failing grade

choices.label: The gap is the size of my update
choices.peek: That is the honest read. A larger gap between what you expected and what you observed means a larger correction to your guess. Small gap, small tweak. Large gap, look at your assumptions. Scientists live inside this feeling.
choices.found: that the size of the gap was the size of your update

choices.label: It depends on how confident I was
choices.peek: Good instinct. If you were sure it would be 24 hours, a 6 hour gap is loud. If you were uncertain to begin with, the same 6 hours is quieter and asks you to run again. Confidence is how loud a gap gets to be.
choices.found: that confidence is how loud a gap gets to be

cards.question: In AP Research you read a single study reporting a small effect on reaction time in a lab task. Before you decide what to do with it, commit: how much should this one study move your working picture of the topic?

choices.label: A lot, because it is a published study
choices.peek: A little too much weight. One study is one measurement, and how much it should move your picture depends on how tight the method was and how much trust you had in your prior view. Trust in the reading, weighed against the size of the surprise, sets the update.
choices.found: that trust weighed against surprise set the size of your update

choices.label: A little, because it is only one study
choices.peek: Calibrated. You are weighting a single reading against everything else you have read on the topic. That is exactly the move: you do not throw out a small piece of evidence, you scale it by how much you trust it against your existing picture.
choices.found: that you scaled the small piece of evidence against your picture

choices.label: Depends on how surprising the result is
choices.peek: That is the whole art. A surprising result from a shaky method should move you little. A surprising result from a careful method should move you more. That move is what statisticians write down in equations.
choices.found: that the move you just made is what statisticians write down in equations

cards.kicker: Names for the moves you already made
cards.question: You have been doing four moves this whole page: commit to a guess, notice the gap, weigh the gap against your confidence, and update. That is the working core of a whole research program. Which name do you want on it first?

choices.label: Prediction error
choices.peek: That is the technical name for the gap you kept noticing. Prediction error is the signed difference between what your model expected and what actually came in. Everything downstream, from the titration to the histogram to the study, was you reading a prediction error and deciding what to do with it.
choices.found: that the gap you kept naming was prediction error

choices.label: Precision
choices.peek: That is the technical name for how loud a gap gets to be. Precision is the inverse of variance, the weight your model puts on a signal. High precision means a small gap is loud and moves you a lot. Low precision means even a big gap gets discounted. You were already doing precision weighting when you asked how confident you were.
choices.found: that how loud a gap got to be was precision weighting

choices.label: Belief update
choices.peek: That is the technical name for the whole cycle: prior expectation, meets prediction error, weighted by precision, yields a new expectation. Written formally it is Bayesian updating, and in the active inference literature the quantity being minimized across those updates is called free energy. You did the update by hand four times on this page.
choices.found: that the four moves on this page were belief updates minimizing free energy

personas.label: For educators
personas.invite: You have run some version of predict, observe, revise a few hundred times already, under whichever textbook name your syllabus prefers. What this page adds is a small clean fork you can lift into a class period tomorrow without any adaptation. The workshop is a door for those who ask, not a pitch.

cards.theme: the two term tradeoff by hand
cards.question: Before a unit test, you can spend one more class period reviewing what students already mostly know, or introducing one new idea that will surprise them. Before we say anything about it, commit: which move usually helps a class more?

choices.label: Review what they mostly know, secure the base
choices.peek: Sometimes the right call, especially with a shaky class. But notice what you just weighed: how much they will learn from a surprising new piece against how much they still need the familiar ground. You do this by feel every planning period, and you almost never write it down.
choices.found: that you weighed familiar ground against a surprising new piece

choices.label: One new idea that will surprise them
choices.peek: Often the higher yield call. Again, the interesting part is what you just balanced without naming it: expected gain from the new material against the cost of leaving safer ground. That balance is the whole shape of good lesson planning.
choices.found: that the balance is the shape of good lesson planning

choices.label: Depends on the class in front of me
choices.peek: That is the honest answer any veteran teacher gives. What the class in front of you sets is the two weights: how much they need certainty right now, and how much a surprise would move them. You already carry those two dials in your head.
choices.found: that you already carry the two dials in your head

cards.question: In an AP Physics lab you can ask students to write the expected value before every trial, or only the observed value. Before we mark one as better, commit: which one changes how students actually learn from the run?

choices.label: Observed value only, that is the data
choices.peek: Cleaner sheet, thinner learning. Without a predicted value column, students never get to be surprised, and without surprise the lab teaches only the answer, not the reasoning. The predict column is where the physics does its work on them.
choices.found: that the predict column is where the physics did its work

choices.label: Expected value first, then observed
choices.peek: That extra column is not busywork. Every gap between expected and observed is a place a student's sense of momentum, or friction, or optics revised itself in real time. The predict column is the whole active part of the lab.
choices.found: that the predict column is the whole active part of the lab

choices.label: Both, but only if they are graded together
choices.peek: You know the shape. Grading only the observed value trains them to fudge; grading the honesty of the predict-observe gap trains them to think. The rubric is the small change that changes everything else.
choices.found: that grading the honesty of the gap changed everything else

cards.kicker: How loud a gap gets to be
cards.question: In AP Statistics your class predicts a mean, then computes it from a sample. Two students get gaps of similar size but very different confidence in their prediction. Before we say what to do next, commit: whose gap is teaching more right now?

choices.label: The confident student, because the surprise is louder
choices.peek: Right on. A student who was very sure and got a moderate gap has a much bigger swing in what they now believe than a student who was unsure and got the same gap. Confidence turns a small numerical difference into a big learning moment, or a shrug.
choices.found: that confidence turned the same numerical gap into a very different moment

choices.label: The unsure student, because they need more help
choices.peek: Their need is real, but the confident student's picture of the world just took a bigger shake and is wide open to being redrawn this minute. Both matter, and knowing which is which is how you spend your next five minutes wisely.
choices.found: that you spent the next five minutes where the picture was wide open

choices.label: It depends on which one asks a question first
choices.peek: Classroom truth. But underneath the question, you are still reading who was confident and who was tentative, and letting the size of that surprise tell you where to lean in. You do this reading in seconds every class.
choices.found: that you did this reading in seconds every class

cards.theme: two ways to shrink a gap
cards.question: When a student's expected value and observed value disagree, they have two moves: change the belief, or change what they measured. Before we say more, commit: which one do you steer them toward first?

choices.label: Change the belief, that is the point of the lab
choices.peek: Most of the time, yes. Updating the model on a well run measurement is what science is for. But sometimes the right move is to change what they measured: run it again, tighten the method, verify the reading. Knowing which case you are in is the teaching.
choices.found: that knowing which case you are in was the teaching

choices.label: Change what they measured, protect the model
choices.peek: There are cases for this: sloppy reading, uncalibrated instrument, contaminated sample. But if the method was clean, retreating to the measurement is how you teach students to defend a wrong model. The fork has to stay honest both ways.
choices.found: that the fork had to stay honest both ways to teach anything

choices.label: Depends on how clean the method was
choices.peek: That is the working teacher's answer. The whole judgment lives in that word clean: was the reading careful, the instrument calibrated, the sample real. Once you have called the method clean, the belief is the honest thing to change.
choices.found: that once the method was clean, the belief was the honest thing to change

cards.theme: the one page fork you can hand a student
cards.kicker: Small enough to fit in a class period
cards.question: You have a lab tomorrow. Before we say what to hand out, commit: which one page piece would actually change how the period runs for you?

choices.label: A predict column added to the existing sheet
choices.peek: The smallest useful change. One column before the observed value, one prompt at the end asking which was bigger: the gap, or how sure you were. Nothing else on your sheet has to move for the period to teach differently.
choices.found: that one column changed how the period taught

choices.label: A short fork the student walks after the gap
choices.peek: Two questions on a card: was the method clean, and how sure was I. Clean method plus a real gap points to changing the belief; unclean method points to running it again. The student learns the fork by walking it, not by hearing it.
choices.found: that the student learned the fork by walking it

choices.label: A one line rubric that grades the honesty of the gap
choices.peek: The rubric that shifts the class. Full credit for a well recorded prediction, a well recorded observation, and an honest note about which was more surprising than expected. Grades stop rewarding fudged data and start rewarding real thinking.
choices.found: that grading the honesty of the gap rewarded real thinking

personas.label: For engineers
personas.invite: You already run tight loops. Predict, measure, compare, adjust. This page is the same loop turned on itself: five short cards where you commit to a guess before the reveal. The fork you will feel is the one you feel every sprint, when to keep probing and when to ship what you have.

cards.question: You are about to run an unfamiliar page. Before it renders anything real, commit: which of these does your gut say it is?

choices.label: A landing page with instrumentation stapled on
choices.peek: Closer than most. This is a working thing that only advances after you commit a guess. The point is not the page, it is that you never open a system blank, you open it with a model already loaded, and the run is what tests that model.
choices.found: that you never open a system blank, you open it with a model already loaded

choices.label: A small deterministic demo I can trace end to end
choices.peek: Reasonable read. It is a small working thing whose only real behavior is forcing a commit before a reveal. What you just did is the same thing you do when you stub out an interface before you read the implementation: write the expectation first, then measure against it.
choices.found: that you wrote the expectation before you measured against it

choices.label: I have no priors on this one
choices.peek: Even that is a prior. You just predicted your own uncertainty, which is what a well calibrated engineer does before a stress test. No priors is itself a shape, and the run will still tell you where that shape was off.
choices.found: that no priors was itself a shape you carried in

cards.question: You held a spec in your head. Before you read what the page actually did, commit: when the trace loads, will it match your spec or drift?

choices.label: Roughly matches, off in the corners
choices.peek: That is usually how it lands. The spec in your head is a compressed model, the trace is the run. The value of reading the trace is finding exactly which corner your compression dropped, so you can widen the model right there and not everywhere.
choices.found: that the value of the trace is finding which corner your compression dropped

choices.label: Drifts in a place I cannot name yet
choices.peek: Trust that instinct. When a spec feels off before you can point at where, the trace is the only fair judge. Reading it is not ceremony, it is the check that lets you name the drift so the next iteration is aimed.
choices.found: that the trace lets you name the drift so the next pass is aimed

choices.label: I already know exactly what it did
choices.peek: Maybe. But the same confidence has hidden every regression you have ever chased at 2am. The habit of peeking anyway is cheap insurance, because a matched trace costs you five seconds and a missed drift costs you a night.
choices.found: that peeking anyway is cheap insurance against a night of chasing

cards.question: The trace and your spec do not fully agree. Before you decide what to do, commit: what is that delta actually worth to you?

choices.label: A defect to close and forget
choices.peek: Flip it. The delta between predicted and observed is the only free information in the loop. Closing it without reading it is throwing away the one signal your test just paid for. The delta tells you where your model was wrong, which is more useful than a green build.
choices.found: that the delta is the only free information in the loop

choices.label: A gap between expected and observed, worth reading before I patch
choices.peek: That is the move. The gap between what you expected and what the system did is your cheapest teacher. Small gap, small correction; large gap, your model was aimed at the wrong axis. Either way you read before you patch, because the read is what makes the patch cheap.
choices.found: that reading before patching is what makes the patch cheap

choices.label: It depends on how much I trust each side
choices.peek: Good instinct. When you trust the observation more, you move your model toward it; when you trust the model more, you look harder at the measurement. That trust-weighting is what stops you from thrashing on noise the moment a flaky sensor shouts.
choices.found: that trust-weighting is what stops you from thrashing on noise

cards.question: The delta points somewhere. Commit before the reveal: with a real deadline and a real gap in hand, which move is right?

choices.label: Widen the search, probe adjacent parts of the model
choices.peek: Sometimes yes. When the delta is large or when the same class of surprise keeps recurring, widening beats patching. You spend a little extra time now to stop paying for the same wrong assumption in every future run. That is exploration, and it is the right call more often than deadlines suggest.
choices.found: that widening now stops you from paying for the same wrong assumption later

choices.label: Change the one thing the delta implicated, rerun, ship
choices.peek: Also often right. When the delta is small and localized, the cheapest move is to touch exactly the piece the surprise pointed at and rerun. That is exploitation of a signal you already paid to receive. The skill is knowing which of these two moves fits this gap.
choices.found: that the skill is knowing which move fits this gap

choices.label: I want a rule that tells me which one
choices.peek: There is no rule, only a felt weighing. The larger the surprise and the shakier your trust in the current model, the more you explore; the smaller and more local, the more you exploit. You already do this every sprint. This card is just naming the fork so you can feel it before you commit.
choices.found: that the fork is felt, not ruled, and naming it is the whole edge

cards.question: Five cards in. Before the exit, commit one last time: what did this page actually cost you, and what did it hand back?

choices.label: A few minutes and a cleaner mental model of my own loop
choices.peek: That is the honest trade. You spent a few minutes committing guesses before reveals, and what you carry out is a slightly sharper picture of the loop you already ran. Not new religion, not a framework to adopt, just your own habit named clearly enough to reuse tomorrow.
choices.found: that your own habit was worth naming clearly enough to reuse tomorrow

choices.label: A working thing that proved its own point
choices.peek: Fair read. The page is small on purpose. It only had to force you to commit before it revealed, five times, so the loop it is describing is a loop you actually ran. Anything less and it would just be a page telling you what a loop is.
choices.found: that the page had to be a loop you ran, not a loop it described

choices.label: Nothing I did not already know

choices.found: that what you knew is now sitting one level closer to the surface

personas.label: For STEAM professionals
personas.invite: You already work with models next to measurements for a living. These five cards run the same posture at a small scale: commit a prediction, read the run, weigh the gap, decide what to do with it. The rungs stay concrete through card three and give the math a name only at the end, opt in.

cards.question: You are about to step through a small walkthrough you have not seen. Before it shows you anything, commit to what you expect. Which does your working intuition say?

choices.label: A structured demo whose behavior is deterministic once I see the setup
choices.peek: Close. The setup is that the walkthrough only advances after you commit a guess, and the mechanism is deterministic once you see it. What just happened is the pattern you already run at the bench: you wrote down your prediction before you took the reading, so the reading can actually update you rather than just confirm you.
choices.found: that a prediction written before the reading is what lets the reading update you

choices.label: A shaped walkthrough where I am the one running the loop on myself
choices.peek: Sharp read. You are the one running the loop, and the interesting variable is the gap between what you committed to and what you find on the other side of the click. Nothing is being measured on you and nothing leaves the page; the reading you compare against is one you own and can throw out.
choices.found: that the interesting variable is a gap you own on both sides

choices.label: I want to hold off until I see one full loop
choices.peek: Also a fair prior. The full loop is five cards and it repeats the same four moves: predict, read, weigh, adjust. Holding off is itself a prior about what the walkthrough is worth, which the walkthrough itself will confirm or push against by card five.
choices.found: that holding off is itself a prior worth watching

cards.question: You have a prior. Before you take the actual reading, commit: when the reading arrives, will your prior survive it intact?

choices.label: Intact on the main axis, off on a detail
choices.peek: That is usually how a good prior lands. Main axis survives, a detail moves. The detail is the interesting bit, because that is the place your prior compressed the system a little too aggressively. Reading the detail is what lets the next observation land tighter.
choices.found: that the detail is where your prior compressed too aggressively

choices.label: The prior will move, I just do not know on which axis
choices.peek: Best posture for a novel setup. When you cannot say ahead of time which axis will move, the value of the reading is not the reading itself, it is which axis the change lands on. That is what a well designed observation buys you: not a value, but a direction.
choices.found: that a well designed observation buys a direction, not just a value

choices.label: The prior was solid, I do not expect movement
choices.peek: Fair, and worth testing. When a prior is stable across multiple readings you get to trust it more, which in the loop language is called earning precision. Precision that has not been earned is confidence that has not been paid for.
choices.found: that precision is confidence that has been paid for

cards.kicker: Turn the gap into a count
cards.question: The reading and your prior do not fully line up. Before you decide what the gap means, commit: how would you turn that gap into something you can count?

choices.label: Log the direction and magnitude, then wait for the next reading
choices.peek: That is the counting move. A gap is a data point with a direction and a magnitude; a second gap in the same direction is where a signal begins to form. That habit, direction plus magnitude across repeated observations, is the shape a Bayesian update takes when you write it out: tallying what actually happened next to what you expected.
choices.found: that tallying direction and magnitude against a prior is the shape a Bayesian update takes

choices.label: Weight the gap by how much I trust each side
choices.peek: That is the precision move. When the instrument is noisy you weight the prior more; when the prior is thin you weight the reading more. In the loop language this weighting is called precision, and it is what stops the update from being either too eager or too stubborn.
choices.found: that precision is what stops updates from being either too eager or too stubborn

choices.label: Compare against a baseline I already trust
choices.peek: That is the calibration move. A gap against a trusted baseline is worth more than a gap against a fresh model, because the baseline has already earned some of its precision. In practice you run all three moves together: log the gap, weight it, compare it against something you already trust.
choices.found: that in practice the three moves run together

cards.question: You have a gap, a direction, and some sense of trust in each side. Before the reveal, commit: what is the disciplined move with a gap of that shape?

choices.label: Rework the whole model to be safe
choices.peek: Almost always the wrong call. When the gap points at a specific axis, moving the whole model is expensive and it also throws away the parts of the model that were fine. The disciplined move is to shift the piece the gap implicated, keep the rest, and let the next observation say whether the shift was enough.
choices.found: that the disciplined move shifts the piece the gap implicated, not the whole model

choices.label: Shift only the parameter the gap implicated, then re-observe
choices.peek: That is the move. Small, cheap updates in the direction the gap pointed at let you run the loop again quickly, which is where the value lives. Two or three fast cycles will tell you more than one heroic revision, because each cycle gives the next reading something specific to disagree with.
choices.found: that fast small cycles tell you more than one heroic revision

choices.label: Hold the model, log the gap, wait for a second reading
choices.peek: Also disciplined, and sometimes exactly right. When a single gap is small and the cost of a wrong shift is real, holding steady and waiting for the second reading is what earns the precision to act. The rule is not shift-fast, the rule is shift only when the count is worth the shift.
choices.found: that you shift only when the count is worth the shift

cards.question: You have run four small predict-read-weigh-update turns. Before the last reveal, commit: what do you want to walk out with?

choices.label: The loop as a working habit, math name optional
choices.peek: That is the honest exit. The habit is: commit a prediction, take the reading, log the gap with direction and magnitude, shift only the piece the gap implicated, repeat. You can run that habit for years without ever writing an equation, and it will still be the shape a Bayesian update takes, whether or not you ever name it that.
choices.found: that the habit is the shape, whether or not you name it

choices.label: The math name on the loop I just ran
choices.peek: Fair opt-in. What you just ran, predict then read then weight-by-trust then update, is aligned with the shape of variational inference under the free energy account: prior meets likelihood, precision weights the update, the whole thing minimizes surprise across repeated turns. You did not need the name to run it, and now you have the name.
choices.found: that the loop you ran is aligned with the shape of variational inference

choices.label: A partner who runs the loop next to me, not on me
choices.peek: That is the offer. Nothing about this walkthrough measures you, scores you, or keeps a record of your clicks; the loop is a shape you can run on your own work, and the closing door is an invitation to keep going with a partner who runs the loop next to you. You stay the one holding the prior and reading the gap.
choices.found: that the partner runs the loop next to you, not on you

choices.peek: That is also fair, and worth respecting. Framing here stays narrow on purpose: no leaps about minds, no leaps about inner states, no leaps about what this page thinks you are. Just the mechanism, next to its caveat, on each card. If the framing feels off, the exit door on card five goes to where the framing is spelled out in full.

choices.label: Cannot tell yet, I want to see it repeat
choices.peek: Best answer of the three. A single gap is a data point; a repeated gap in the same direction is a signal. This loop shows up again on the next card, so you can watch whether the direction is stable or drifts. That is the test you were about to demand anyway.

cards.question: The claim so far is that predict, read, weigh is a loop worth running in the open. Commit before the reveal: what would have to happen for that claim to be wrong?

choices.label: The loop would have to fail when the direction is repeated

personas.label: For journalists
personas.invite: You already run this loop under a different name: form the working theory, ask the question that could break it, read what actually came back, adjust. This short walk is a small on-the-record demonstration of the same loop, with the receipts visible as you go. The exit door lands on the transparency page, not a pitch.

cards.theme: the working theory, before the call
cards.question: You are about to interview a source you have never met on a story you have half-shaped. Before the call connects, commit: what are you actually carrying in with you?

choices.label: A working theory I plan to test, not defend
choices.peek: That is the honest read of the job. The theory is a scaffold, not a verdict, and the interview is the check. This walk is the same shape: you commit to a guess, then read what actually came back, then decide what the gap means.
choices.found: that the theory was scaffold for the check, not a verdict

choices.label: A rough model of the source and the story
choices.peek: Right. You always carry a model in, even when you tell yourself you do not, because a truly blank interview has no follow-ups. The walk makes that model visible for one moment so you can see the shape of it before you look at the reply.
choices.found: that a truly blank interview would have no follow-ups

choices.label: Questions I want on the record no matter what they say
choices.peek: That list is a form of guess too. Each question guesses at a class of answer worth having; the interview then tells you which guesses held. The walk uses the same move, with the guess saved before the peek.
choices.found: that each question guessed at a class of answer worth having

cards.question: The reply arrives. Before you decide what to lead with, commit: what are you actually doing when you read it against the theory you brought in?

choices.label: Sorting what confirmed, what surprised, and what is missing
choices.peek: That triage is the whole read. Confirmations are the model surviving; surprises are the corrections; missing pieces are the next questions. This walk does the same triage in miniature and lets you see it happen on your own guesses.
choices.found: that surprises are the corrections and gaps are the next questions

choices.label: Checking whether the surprise is signal or performance
choices.peek: That is the discipline. Not every surprise is a correction; some are a source performing a version of themselves. The walk cannot tell you the difference, but it can show you the move of holding surprise open long enough to ask.
choices.found: that holding surprise open long enough to ask was the move

choices.label: Weighing the reply against the sources you already have
choices.peek: That weighing is how a working theory earns its keep. Each reply either raises or lowers your confidence in the version you brought in, and a working reporter carries that running weight across the whole story, not just the last call.
choices.found: that the reply raised or lowered your confidence in the version you brought in

cards.question: You have a real gap in hand between what you expected and what the source actually said. Before you spend the next hour on it, commit: which move is more likely to be the story?

choices.label: Triangulate: pull a second and third source against the gap
choices.peek: That is the harder move, and usually the right one. Triangulation treats the gap as a claim to be checked against independent readings, and it protects you from a single source setting your model. It is the loop working against itself.
choices.found: that triangulation was the loop working against itself

choices.label: Follow the source into the gap and see where it leads
choices.peek: There is a version of this move that is honest reporting and a version that quietly hands your model to the source. The walk cannot tell you which you are doing, but naming the fork out loud is often what keeps the difference visible.
choices.found: that naming the fork out loud kept the difference visible

choices.label: Do both in parallel and keep them on separate lines
choices.peek: That is the discipline of a good desk. Following and triangulating are different jobs, and mixing them collapses the check. The walk mirrors the same discipline: guess, peek, compare, and never let the peek rewrite what you guessed.
choices.found: that the peek was not allowed to rewrite the guess

cards.theme: two questions and the counting behind them

choices.label: It is counting plus a rule for updating the guess
choices.peek: That is the second half. The count gives you the numerator and denominator; the rule says the guess should move toward the reply in proportion to how surprising the reply was. Small surprise, small move; large surprise, larger move.

choices.label: It is a receipt anyone can audit against my write-up

choices.found: that the ledger was the same shape as source notes, only kept out loud

cards.theme: the door that opens onto the record

choices.label: To check whether the receipts they showed you match the receipts they show everyone

choices.label: To see whether this loop scales past a five-card demo

cards.question: Think of the last morning you walked into their room. Before you said hello, before they said anything, you already had a small sense of how the day was going to go. Which of these felt closest to how that sense arrived?

cards.theme: the parable structure, without the parable

cards.question: Something the bed showed you landed a little off from your picture. Commit before you look closer: is that gap a mistake in your tending, or is it the bed telling you something you could not have known yesterday?

choices.label: A gap means I tended it wrong
choices.peek: Gently flip it. A gap between your picture and what the bed did is not a mark against you, it is the bed telling you exactly what the night gave it. The bigger the surprise, the more it just told you.
choices.found: that the bigger the surprise, the more the bed just told you

choices.label: The gap is the bed telling me something
choices.peek: Right. The difference between what you pictured and what the bed showed is quiet information. A morning that matches your picture perfectly teaches you nothing new; the mismatch is where the small daily notice actually lives.
choices.found: that the mismatch is where the small daily notice lives

choices.label: Depends how big the gap is
choices.peek: Good calibration. The size of the gap is the size of the message: a small surprise is a small note, a large one asks you to look longer today. Either way it is information, never a grade on your care.
choices.found: that the size of the gap is the size of the message

cards.question: The bed gave you a small note. Commit before you decide: what is the gentlest move with a note this size?

choices.label: Redo the whole bed to be safe
choices.peek: Rarely needed. The note already pointed at one small thing to attend to, so you attend to that and look again tomorrow, not the rest. Tending is just closing the small gap gently, again the next day, and the day after.
choices.found: that tending is closing the small gap gently, day after day

choices.label: Attend to the one thing the note pointed at, and look again tomorrow
choices.peek: That is the move. You attend to the piece the surprise pointed at, look again the next morning, and read the new note. Do it in tight small passes and your picture stays close to the bed, because you never let the gap grow strange.
choices.found: that tight small passes keep the picture close to the bed

choices.label: Sit with it a day, look again before deciding
choices.peek: Sitting with it is part of the practice too. You are giving the picture a second morning to be read against, so the small change you make tomorrow is a truer one. Waiting one more day is not delay, it is listening a beat longer.
choices.found: that waiting one more day is listening a beat longer

cards.question: You ran the same short circuit four times: bring a picture, look at the bed, notice the gap, attend to the one thing. Before the last reveal, commit: is that circuit only for beginner gardeners, or is it what any small daily practice is, under the names?

choices.label: Only for when you are learning
choices.peek: It never stops being the practice. Bring a picture, look, notice, attend is not scaffolding you outgrow; it is the shape of any small daily practice held gently. Anyone who tends anything runs it, whether they name it or not.
choices.found: that the practice never stops being the practice

choices.label: It is what a small daily practice already is
choices.peek: That is it. Bring a picture, look, notice, attend, gently and often, is what a small daily practice always has been under the names. We run the same small circuit in the open, out loud, and we show the notes we get instead of hiding them.
choices.found: that we run the same small circuit in the open

choices.label: It is one small circuit among many I already keep
choices.peek: You already keep several. This is the shape that quietly runs under them: a soft picture, a real look, a small notice, one gentle attend. Naming the shape does not change your practice; it just gives you words for what you were already doing.
choices.found: that naming the shape does not change the practice

personas.label: For community organizers
personas.invite: You already run a loop out there: you listen to a neighborhood, you test a small thing with a few people, you read what came back, you adjust. This is a small page that names that loop plainly. It asks you to guess before it shows you anything, because that is what a good door-knock does anyway.

cards.question: Think of the last block you canvassed, or the last kitchen-table meeting you sat in. Commit before you keep reading: did you walk in blank, or did you walk in with a working guess about what people would say?

choices.label: I walked in with a working guess
choices.peek: That is honest organizing. You never arrive blank on a block, you arrive with a working guess built from the last block, and you let the conversations correct it. This page runs the same shape, only the block is a screen.
choices.found: that you arrive with a working guess, not blank

choices.label: I tried to listen without assumptions
choices.peek: Even that is a guess. You predicted that assumptions would get in the way, so you held them lightly on purpose. That is still a model, held quietly. The best listeners on your team are the ones who know they are holding one.
choices.found: that even open listening carries a quiet model

choices.label: Depends on the block and who was already there
choices.peek: Good calibration. You always adjust the guess to the block and the folks who were already organizing there. You never use one guess for every door. That is the craft, and it is the same craft this page runs on.
choices.found: that the guess always adjusts to the block and the folks already there

cards.theme: read what the block gave back
cards.question: You made the read. Before you look at what the conversations actually gave back, commit again: did the block match the working guess, or did it slide off in a direction your team did not expect?

choices.label: Close enough, roughly what we pictured
choices.peek: Reading the block is the check. The working guess your team brought was a model; the conversations are the run. Reading the run against the guess is not paperwork, it is the only way to find where the two stopped agreeing.
choices.found: that reading the run is the only way to find where the guess and the block parted

choices.label: Off somewhere we did not name yet
choices.peek: That instinct is worth trusting. You cannot know how the working guess was wrong until you look at what the block actually said, not what you assumed they would say. The peek is you opening the notes instead of trusting the plan.
choices.found: that you opened the notes instead of trusting the plan

choices.label: Different blocks, different answers, always
choices.peek: Good calibration. You already treat every block as its own reading, not a copy of the last one. That habit is what keeps the team honest when the campaign starts to want to hear one story.
choices.found: that treating every block as its own reading keeps the team honest

cards.theme: the gap is the organizing signal
cards.question: The block gave back something off from your working guess. Commit before you look closer: is that gap a failure of your team, or is it the most useful thing on your clipboard?

choices.label: A gap means we read the block wrong
choices.peek: Flip it. A gap between the working guess and what the block actually said is not a verdict on your team, it is a reading that points exactly at the part of the guess that needed work. The bigger the surprise, the more it just told you.
choices.found: that the bigger the surprise, the more the block just told you

choices.label: The gap is the useful part
choices.peek: Right. The difference between what your team expected and what people actually said is pure signal. A canvass that matches the working guess perfectly teaches you nothing new; the mismatch is where the next campaign lives.
choices.found: that the mismatch is where the next campaign lives

choices.label: Depends how big the gap is
choices.peek: Good calibration. The size of the gap is the size of the message: a small surprise is a small correction, a large one says your working guess was aimed wrong. Either way it is data pointing somewhere, never a mark against the team.
choices.found: that the size of the gap is the size of the message

cards.theme: adjust the one thing, then test again
cards.question: You have a real gap in hand and it is pointing somewhere on the block. Commit before you decide: what is the smartest move for a team with a gap this size?

choices.label: Rewrite the whole campaign to be safe
choices.peek: Rarely worth it. The gap already told your team which part of the guess was off, so you adjust that piece and test again with a few doors, not the whole plan. In plain terms, a small mismatch calls for a small update, not a new strategy.
choices.found: that a small mismatch calls for a small update, not a new strategy

choices.label: Adjust the one thing the gap pointed at, then test with a few doors again
choices.peek: That is the move. You change the piece the surprise pointed at, run it past a few more doors, and read the new gap. Do it in tight cheap passes and the campaign tracks the block closely, because the team never lets the gap grow stale. Prediction and correction, at the size of a neighborhood.
choices.found: that tight cheap passes keep the campaign tracking the block

choices.label: Bring the gap back to the folks already on the block and let them shape the fix
choices.peek: That is solidarity in the loop. The people already organizing on that block hold information your team does not. You bring them the gap, they shape the update, then you test again together. The correction is smaller and truer because it was built with, not for.
choices.found: that the correction is smaller and truer when built with, not for

cards.theme: name the loop your team already runs
cards.question: You ran the same short circuit four times: working guess, read the block, size the gap, adjust one thing. Before the last reveal, commit: is that circuit a training exercise, or is it what good organizing has always been, under the names?

choices.label: A training exercise for new organizers
choices.peek: It never stops being the work. Listen, observe, adjust, test again is not a training-wheel loop; it is what any team that keeps its ear to the block is already doing. In plain language, your team is running prediction and correction on a neighborhood, in solidarity, out loud.
choices.found: that the loop is what any team keeping its ear to the block is already doing

choices.label: It is what good organizing already is
choices.peek: That is it. Listen, observe, adjust, test again, cheaply and often, is what good organizing has always been under the names. Prediction and correction at the size of a block, in solidarity. We run this same loop in the open on the hardest thing you can hand us, and we show our gaps instead of hiding them.
choices.found: that we run this same loop in the open on the hardest thing you can hand us

choices.label: It is the same loop other trades already run under other names
choices.peek: That is exactly right. Builders, gardeners, medics, teachers, organizers, all run some version of a working guess, a real reading, a sized gap, a small adjust. In plainer names it is prediction and correction, at whatever size the work asks for. Your team already runs it at the size of a block, in solidarity.
choices.found: that every trade runs some version of prediction and correction

personas.label: For farmers
personas.invite: You already read fields the way most people read a book. Weather, soil, animals, the price sheet, all held at once. Come in with a season in mind and see if the shape of it lands.

cards.question: It is the morning you walk the ground before you decide anything. Before you look at the sky or the dirt, commit: what are you actually doing on that walk?

choices.label: Checking a list in my head
choices.peek: It looks like a checklist, but that is not quite it. You are carrying a picture of how the field should look for this week of this year, and you are letting your eyes find where the real field is off from the picture. The walk is the compare.
choices.found: that the walk is a compare against the picture in your head

choices.label: Looking for what feels wrong
choices.peek: That is closer to the truth of it. You hold a rough idea of what right looks like for this ground, this season, this weather, and your eye snags on the part that does not fit. What feels wrong is the gap between your picture and the field.
choices.found: that what feels wrong is the gap between your picture and the field

choices.label: Just walking, I sort it out later
choices.peek: Even that is doing the work. You are not blank out there. Years of ground under your boots gave you a picture of how this field runs, and the walk lets that picture bump up against today's version. The sorting happens because the bumps show up.
choices.found: that the walk lets your picture bump up against today's field

cards.question: You are about to pull a soil sample from the low corner. Before the lab comes back, commit to a guess: what will the numbers say about that corner?

choices.label: Low on nitrogen, wet, tight
choices.peek: You just wrote a spec for that corner before the lab did. That is not a small thing. When the numbers come back you will know exactly where your read was right and where the ground surprised you, and the surprise is worth more than a matching result.
choices.found: that the surprise is worth more than a matching result

choices.label: About the same as the middle, honestly
choices.peek: Good, that is a real prediction. If the lab comes back and the corner reads the same, your model of that ground held up and you saved yourself a treatment. If it comes back different, you just learned where you were reading the field wrong.
choices.found: that a matching result confirms your read of the ground

choices.label: I would rather wait for the lab
choices.peek: Fair, and worth flipping. If you commit to a guess first, the lab result stops being just a number and starts being a message: here is where you and the ground still agree, and here is where you did not know it had changed.
choices.found: that a guess turns the lab result into a message

cards.theme: the gap tells you where to look
cards.question: The lab came back and the corner is not what you called. Before you decide what it means, commit: is that gap a knock on your judgment, or the most useful line on the sheet?

choices.label: It means my read was off
choices.peek: It says one specific part of your read was off, not the whole eye. The gap is a pointer: something changed in that corner since the last time you walked it closely, and the number just told you where to look. That is a favor, not a mark against you.
choices.found: that the gap is a pointer, not a mark against your eye

choices.label: The gap is the useful part
choices.peek: That is the read. When your picture and the ground match, the lab told you what you already knew. When they do not match, the sheet just paid for itself, because it pointed at the exact patch of ground where your model is behind reality.
choices.found: that the gap paid for the sheet by pointing at what changed

choices.label: Depends how big the gap is
choices.peek: Good calibration. A small gap is a small nudge, adjust and move on. A large one says something about that corner shifted more than you thought, drainage, compaction, a season of a cover crop that did more than you expected. Big surprise, big message.
choices.found: that the size of the gap is the size of the message

cards.question: You have a real gap in that corner and it is pointing somewhere. Before you plan the season, commit: what is the smart move with a signal this size?

choices.label: Overhaul the whole rotation to be safe
choices.peek: Rarely worth it. The gap already told you which piece is off, so you treat that piece, watch it for a season, and read the ground again. Big moves feel like control, but the ground does not answer overhauls, it answers small honest passes you can read.
choices.found: that the ground answers small honest passes, not overhauls

choices.label: Adjust the one thing the sample pointed at, then check next season
choices.peek: That is the move a good apprentice learns first. You change what the signal actually implicated, one pass on that corner, and you walk it again with a fresh guess in mind. Tight cheap passes and honest walks are how your read of the ground stays current.
choices.found: that tight cheap passes keep your read of the ground current

choices.label: Ask the neighbor who farmed this ground before me
choices.peek: Do it. Tacit knowledge from the last hands on this dirt is a reading you cannot get from a lab sheet. Their picture plus your picture plus the number is a better model than any one of them alone, and the corner has been talked about before.
choices.found: that the last hands on the ground carry a reading no sheet has

cards.question: Predict what the ground will say, peek at what it says, size the gap, adjust one thing, walk it again. Before the last card turns, commit: is that circuit something new, or is it what a good farmer has always done?

choices.label: It is what a good farmer has always done
choices.peek: That is it. The names are new, the shape is old ground. What we call it plainly is a loop: Listen to the field, Observe against your picture, Orchestrate one small change, Partner with the ground and the neighbors on the read. Same work, said plain.
choices.found: that the loop is old ground with a plainer name

choices.label: It is a habit I use when I am learning a new field
choices.peek: It never stops being the work. Fresh ground makes you walk it more carefully, but you never grow out of predict, peek, size the gap, adjust. Skilled hands run this tighter, not fewer times, and the ground keeps changing enough that no farmer is ever finished learning it.
choices.found: that skilled hands run this tighter, never fewer times

choices.label: Something my grandfather did without calling it anything
choices.peek: That is exactly right, and the name does not matter to the ground. What matters is you keep walking, keep guessing, keep sizing the surprise, and keep making the smallest true change. That work carries between generations because the ground rewards it every season.
choices.found: that the ground rewards this work every season, name or no name

personas.label: For tradespeople
personas.invite: You already work the way this page is built: measure, cut, check, adjust, no drama about it. Come in with a real job in mind and see if the shape of it lands the way your work does.

cards.question: You have the piece on the horses and the tape in your hand. Before you mark the line, commit: why do you measure the second time?

choices.label: Because I might have misread the first
choices.peek: That is it, plain. The second measure is not a lack of confidence, it is you catching your own first read before the saw does. The tape does not cost you anything, the cut costs you the piece.
choices.found: that the second measure catches the first read before the saw does

choices.label: Because the tape can shift
choices.peek: Right, and more than the tape. Your eye at the mark, your body at the tape, the piece under the light, all of it moves a hair between reads. Measuring twice is not doubt, it is you giving the same job two independent looks so the wrong one does not win.
choices.found: that two independent looks keep the wrong one from winning

choices.label: Habit, honestly
choices.peek: Best kind of habit. It is the habit of not trusting a single read on anything that cannot be uncut. Every trade has some version of it, and the ones who skip it hand you the stories.
choices.found: that not trusting a single read is the habit of the trades

cards.question: You just made the mark. Before the blade touches the wood, commit: what is the mark actually doing sitting there in pencil?

choices.label: It is where the cut goes
choices.peek: Close, but it is more like the plan for where the cut goes. You are saying, in advance and out loud in pencil, this is where the piece needs to land. When the blade runs, you will know within a hair how right the plan was.
choices.found: that the mark is the plan in pencil for where the cut lands

choices.label: It is the plan I am about to test with the saw
choices.peek: That is the read. The mark is the plan, the cut is the test. If the piece drops into place clean, your plan was true. If it fights, the mark and the material were not agreeing about something, and the fight is telling you which one.
choices.found: that the mark is the plan, the cut is the test

choices.label: A promise to my future self about where the piece lives
choices.peek: Nice frame. The mark is a note from present-you to five-minutes-from-now-you, saying this is where the piece needs to be. Future-you finds out whether present-you was right the moment the piece lands or does not land clean.
choices.found: that the mark is a note from present-you to future-you

cards.kicker: When the piece will not seat
cards.question: You made the cut and the piece is a hair proud of where it should sit. Before you decide what happened, commit: is that hair a mistake, or is it the piece talking?

choices.label: I cut it wrong
choices.peek: Maybe. Or the material moved on you, or the reference edge was not as square as you trusted. A tight fit that will not seat is the piece pointing at exactly one thing that did not agree, and that pointer is worth more than a clean cut with no information.
choices.found: that a piece that will not seat is pointing at what did not agree

choices.label: The piece is telling me something
choices.peek: That is the ear you build over years. The gap between where the piece wants to sit and where it does sit is a reading. Learn to size it and it tells you whether it is the cut, the reference, the material, or the fit you designed. Every hair means something specific.
choices.found: that every hair off is a specific message from the piece

choices.label: Depends how proud it is
choices.peek: Good, that is a tradesperson's answer. A hair is a shave and go, a sixteenth is check the reference, an eighth is the piece or the plan was wrong somewhere real. The size of the gap tells you which tool to reach for, not the same one every time.
choices.found: that the size of the gap tells you which tool to reach for

cards.question: The piece is proud by a hair and the job is not waiting. Before you move, commit: which is the honest move for a gap this size?

choices.label: Force it, it will settle
choices.peek: It will not settle, it will show later. A piece forced into a spot it did not fit puts a stress into the assembly that surfaces the day the trim goes on or the seasons turn. Every trade learns this, usually the hard way, and the good ones only learn it once.
choices.found: that a forced fit surfaces later, always

choices.label: Trim the hair off, dry-fit, then commit
choices.peek: That is the move. You take the gap the piece just showed you, take that much off, dry-fit to check your read was right, and then commit. It is the same short circuit as measure, cut, check, adjust, run one more time because the piece asked you to.
choices.found: that trim, dry-fit, then commit is measure and check run one more time

choices.label: Pull it, remeasure the reference, cut a fresh one
choices.peek: If the material allows it, yes. When the gap says the reference was off, no amount of trimming the piece will fix the piece behind it. Going back to the reference is not starting over, it is you catching that the plan was wrong upstream of the cut.
choices.found: that going back to the reference catches a plan that was wrong upstream

cards.question: Step back from the horses for a second. You just ran the shape four times: mark, cut, read the gap, trim and seat. Before you walk into the rest of this page, commit: what is that shape, honestly?

choices.label: It is just how the work gets done
choices.peek: That is the truest answer on the page. The shape is not a method somebody sold you, it is what the trade does to itself over years so the pieces land clean. Every good tradesperson runs it without naming it, which is why it is worth naming once so you can see it.
choices.found: that the loop is what the trade does to itself so pieces land clean

choices.label: It is the same loop, just tighter each time
choices.peek: That is the shape exactly. Mark, cut, check, adjust, and every pass the gap shrinks because you learned something from the last one. The trade is not one big correct move, it is a short loop run honestly until the piece seats.
choices.found: that the trade is a short loop run honestly until the piece seats

choices.label: It is how you stay honest with the material
choices.peek: Yes. The material does not care what you meant, it only shows you what actually happened. The loop is you letting the material grade your last move and adjusting before the next one, which is the whole difference between a trade and a guess.
choices.found: that the loop is the material grading your last move

personas.label: For writers
personas.invite: You already work with a reader you cannot see. You guess how a line will land, read it back, and adjust. Come in with a page you are stuck on and see if the shape of it lands.

cards.kicker: Before you write the next sentence
cards.question: You are about to draft a line. Before it lands on the page, commit: who is reading it, and what are you predicting they will do with it?

choices.label: One reader I can picture, and I know how they will read it
choices.peek: Then the sentence is not just going onto the page, it is going through a model you are already running. You wrote it because you predicted a certain reaction, an eye slowing here, a small yes there. Every line is a small bet placed on that reader.
choices.found: that every line is a small bet placed on a reader you already model

choices.label: Some average reader, I keep it vague
choices.peek: Worth flipping. A vague reader gives you a vague sentence. Pick one, even a made-up one, and the line sharpens because you know whose eye you are writing for. The reader in your head is the only reader the draft can actually reach.
choices.found: that the reader in your head is the only reader the draft can reach

choices.label: Honestly I write it and see what happens
choices.peek: Even that has a reader tucked inside it. You will read the line back in a minute, and that reading you is a model of a stranger seeing it fresh. You never write into pure blank, you always write into some picture of who is on the other side of it.
choices.found: that you never write into blank, always into a picture of a reader

cards.question: You wrote the line and now you are reading it. Before you decide anything about it, commit: what is the read actually for?

choices.label: Catching typos
choices.peek: That is a floor, not the point. The real read is you playing the reader you predicted, seeing where the line does what you hoped and where it does not. Typos are a bonus. The read is the check against your own bet.
choices.found: that the read is a check against the bet you placed

choices.label: Seeing if it does what I meant it to do
choices.peek: That is the read. You wrote the line believing it would slow the eye here or push the reader forward there, and reading it back is you seeing whether that plan survived contact with the actual page. Meaning it does not put it on the page, doing it does.
choices.found: that meaning it does not put it on the page, doing it does

choices.label: Hearing how it sounds
choices.peek: Yes, and sound is a signal too. The ear catches the beat your inner reader would trip on before the mind can name it. When the rhythm goes off, something in the line disagreed with the sentence you thought you wrote, even if the words look fine.
choices.found: that the ear catches disagreement before the mind can name it

cards.theme: the gap between meant and did
cards.kicker: When the line does not do what you meant
cards.question: You read the line back and it did not do what you wanted. Before you touch it, commit: is that gap a problem with the sentence, or is it the most useful reading you got today?

choices.label: The sentence is broken
choices.peek: The sentence is not broken, it is just honest. It did what the words on the page actually do, and it told you where your idea and the words were not the same thing yet. That gap is the exact spot the next draft has to move.
choices.found: that the gap is the exact spot the next draft has to move

choices.label: The gap is what I needed to see
choices.peek: That is the read. The distance between what you meant and what the line actually did is pure signal. A sentence that lands perfectly teaches you nothing you did not already know. The one that misses tells you where the seam is.
choices.found: that the miss tells you where the seam is

choices.label: Depends how far off it landed
choices.peek: Good calibration. A small miss is a word swap or a comma. A big miss says the sentence and the sentence you thought you were writing were not the same sentence, and you have to decide which one is right for the page. Big gap, real decision.
choices.found: that the size of the miss says how deep the decision is

cards.theme: voice vs clarity, cut vs keep
cards.question: The line is doing something you love but the reader you pictured just tripped on it. Before the next pass, commit: what is the honest move with a gap like this?

choices.label: Keep it, the reader will catch up
choices.peek: Sometimes true, mostly a story we tell ourselves. If the reader you actually predicted tripped, that is data, not a failing on their part. The line that sounds most yours in your head can also be the one the page cannot support yet.
choices.found: that a trip from the predicted reader is data, not their failing

choices.label: Cut it and rewrite for the clarity
choices.peek: Often the move, but do it with your ear on. The rewrite is not a punishment for the sentence you loved, it is the same short circuit again: guess how the new line will land, read it back, size the new gap, adjust. Voice comes back the same way it came the first time.
choices.found: that voice comes back the same way it came the first time

choices.label: Keep the shape, swap one word, read again
choices.peek: That is the small pass. The gap the reader tripped on is usually one hinge word, not the whole sentence. Change the hinge, read the line back with your predicted reader on your shoulder, and see if the new gap is smaller. Do it cheap, do it often.
choices.found: that changing one hinge word is the cheapest honest pass

cards.question: Guess how a line will land, read it back cold, size the gap between meant and did, change one thing, read it again. Before the last reveal, commit: is that circuit something new, or is it what drafting has always been?

choices.label: It is what drafting has always been
choices.peek: That is it. The names are new dress on old work. Plainly it is a loop: Listen to the reader you predicted, Observe the line cold, Orchestrate one small change, Partner with the page instead of forcing it. Every writer who kept getting better ran it, whether or not they named it.
choices.found: that every writer who kept getting better ran this loop, named or not

choices.label: A habit I use when a piece is not working
choices.peek: It never leaves. When the work is going well the loop runs so fast it feels like flow, but it is still running under the ease. When the work gets hard the loop just gets slower and more visible, and that is not a step down, it is the same craft asking to be seen.
